'''''Tilia'' × ''europaea''''', generally known as the '''European lime''',<ref>{{Cite web |title=European Linden Tree Facts |url=https://homeguides.sfgate.com/european-linden-tree-74388.html |access-date=2022-08-21 |website=Home Guides {{!}} SF Gate |language=en}}</ref> '''common lime''' (British Isles) or '''common linden''', is a naturally occurring [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] between ''[[Tilia cordata]]'' (small-leaved lime) and ''[[Tilia platyphyllos]]'' (large-leaved lime). It occurs in the wild in Europe at scattered localities wherever the two parent species are both [[native plant|native]].<ref name=rushforth>Rushforth, K. (1999). ''Trees of Britain and Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-220013-9}}.</ref> It is not closely related to the [[lime (fruit)|lime]] fruit tree, a [[citrus]] species.

==Description==

''Tilia'' × ''europaea''<!-- hybrid symbol not italicised--> is a large [[deciduous]] [[tree]] up to {{convert|15|-|50|m|ft|0|abbr=off}} tall with a trunk up to {{convert|2.5|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}<!-- circumference or diameter??? -->. The base of the trunk often features [[Burl|burr]]s and a dense mass of brushwood.<ref>[[Alan Mitchell (botanist)|Alan Mitchell]], The Field Guide to the Trees of Britain and Northern Europe, William Collins & Co Ltd 1974, {{ISBN|0-00-219213-6}} (p.359)</ref> The [[leaves]] are intermediate between the parents, {{convert|6|–|15|cm|6=0|abbr=off}} long and {{convert|6|–|12|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} broad, thinly hairy below with tufts of denser hairs in the leaf vein axils. The [[flower]]s are produced in clusters of four to ten in early summer with a leafy yellow-green subtending bract; they are fragrant, and pollinated by [[bee]]s. The [[floral formula]] is ✶ K5 C5 A0+5<sup>∞</sup> {{underline|G}}(5).<ref name="craene">{{Cite book| publisher = Cambridge University Press| isbn = 978-0-521-49346-8| last = Ronse De Craene| first = Louis P.| title = Floral Diagrams: An Aid to Understanding Flower Morphology and Evolution| location = Cambridge| date = 2010-02-04| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=24p-LgWPA50C| page = 225}}</ref> The [[fruit]] is a dry nut-like drupe {{convert|8|mm|in|1|frac=8}} in diameter, downy and faintly ribbed.<ref name=rushforth/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Common limes in the landscape, Kings Somborne, UK.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Common limes (foreground) in the landscape of [[King's Somborne]], United Kingdom]]

This hybrid is very widely cultivated, being readily and inexpensively propagated by [[layering (horticulture)|layering]]; as a result, it is often the commonest ''Tilia'' species in urban areas and along [[avenue (landscape)|avenues]] and streets. It is not however the best species for this purpose, as it produces abundant stem sprouts, and also often hosts heavy [[aphid]] populations resulting in [[Honeydew (secretion)|honeydew]] deposits on everything underneath the trees. Furthermore, there is substantial leaf litter in autumn.<ref name=rushforth/>

===Notable trees===
One long-lived example was the "Malmvik lime", planted as a sapling near the Malmvik Manor in [[Stockholm]], Sweden in 1618. The tree existed for 381 years until the last part of the tree fell in a storm in 1999.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bengtsson |first= Rune|date= Winter 2004 |title=The Malmvik Lime: An Historical and Biological Analysis of the Oldest Documented Planting of Common Lime (Tilia x Europaea L.) in Sweden |jstor= 4150380|journal= Garden History|publisher= The Garden History Society |volume=32 |issue= 2|pages= 188–196|doi= 10.2307/4150380}}</ref> The UK [[Tree Register]] Champion is at [[Aysgarth, Yorkshire]], measuring {{Convert|26|m|abbr=on}} in height and {{Convert|295|cm|ftin|abbr=on}} [[diameter at breast height]] in 2009.<ref name=Johnson>Johnson, O. (2011). ''Champion Trees of Britain & Ireland''.  p.165. Kew publishing, Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, London.</ref> The [[:de:Schlosslinde Augustusburg|tree in front of Augustusburg Hunting Lodge in Saxony]] was planted in 1421 according to the chronicles of Augustusburg.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Lemke|first=Karl|title=Naturdenkmale Bäume, Felsen, Wasserfälle|date=1988|others=Hartmut Müller|isbn=978-3-350-00284-9|edition=1. Aufl|location=Berlin|oclc=75004491}}</ref>
Some 13 limes were planted at Mullary cemetery Co Louth Ireland to commemorate "king Billy's" victory at the battle of the Boyne in circa 1669 as lime are not native to Ireland and they were planted to mark the foreign victory, they remain standing today. The [[:de:Murtenlinde|Murten lime tree]] was planted in Fribourg, Switzerland, in 1470 and survived until 1985. A few years before it died, cuttings were taken and planted in various locations from 1985 onwards. According to legend, the historic lime tree is said to commemorate the Swiss Confederates’ victory at the [[Battle of Morat]]. That is why it is known today as the Murten lime tree (Murtenlinde, (German) or [[:fr:Tilleul de Morat|Tilleul de Morat]] (French)).

==Uses==
The leaves, except for their stalks, can be eaten raw.<ref>{{cite book |last=Mabey |first=Richard |title=Food for Free |publisher=Collins |year=2012 |isbn=978-000-743847-1 |location=London |pages=57 |author-link=Richard Mabey}}</ref>

The flowers are used in tea, producing a mildly relaxing effect.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |pages=42}}</ref>

The wood of the lime was commonly used by [[Viking]]s in their [[shield]]s.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}<!--Neil Price talked about this in a ''Wired'' video but not in print?-->
